articles.title: Ethiopia Key Message Update, July 2026 - January 2027: El Niño-driven rainfall delays and deficits raise concerns for the meher harvest
articles.description: Country: Ethiopia Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Millions of households countrywide are struggling to meet their food needs as the June to August lean season peaks amid high market dependence, constrained income, and high food prices. Of particular concern are internally displaced persons (IDPs), refugees, and crop-dependent households that have been atypically market dependent since January. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are widespread as limited food and income access drives food consumption deficits. Rainfall in July supported planting, and widespread crop failure is not currently the most likely scenario; the meher harvest is expected to support Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes beginning in October across many northern, central, and southern areas, although below-average production will likely limit the scale and duration of improvement . FEWS NET will continue to monitor rainfall performance, planting progress, and crop development over the coming weeks. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 across most southern, southeastern, and far-northern pastoral areas as poor livestock productivity, reduced herd sizes, and high food prices constrain food and income access. In northern pastoral areas, poor July to September karan / karma rainfall is anticipated to limit seasonal improvements in pasture and water availability and livestock body conditions, increasing the risk for further herd size declines. Pasture availability is already below average, and according to key informants, a failed rainy season will likely result in depleted pasture within two months. In southern and southeastern areas, the forecast above-average October to December deyr / hageya rains are unlikely to drive immediate improvements in livestock productivity and income despite improving pasture and water conditions, as recovery from prior drought years remains slow due to low herd sizes. Additionally, above-average rains increase the risk of flooding and the likelihood of related displacement and livelihood constraints. El Niño continues to suppress rainfall during the critical June/July to September kiremt/karan/karma season, and full agricultural recovery is increasingly unlikely in the worst-affected northern and eastern areas following severe early-season rainfall deficits and delayed onset. Through the first three weeks of July, rainfall deficits delayed onset by up to four weeks in parts of Amhara and by around three weeks in parts of Afar, northern Somali, and eastern Oromia, while a late start and persistent rainfall deficits drove exceptionally poor seasonal rainfall across northern and eastern Tigray. Across much of the country,the June to July period was the driest on record , with rainfall deficits ranging from roughly 40 to 70 percent of typical across northern, eastern, and central Ethiopia. Improved rainfall in late July partially eased dryness, improved soil moisture, and supported increased planting, reducing the likelihood of widespread crop failure, but the rainfall likely arrived too late to fully offset planting delays, crop damage, and the shortened growing period**.** Below-average and poorly distributed rainfall is forecast through September, with further dry spells likely to constrain soil-moisture recharge and crop development , particularly of eastern Amhara, eastern Tigray, and Afar, where deficits are deepest and the seasonal rainfall window closes rapidly. A below-average meher harvest is most likely across northern and eastern cropping areas, with the greatest losses likely in eastern Amhara, eastern Tigray, and the East and West Hararghe lowlands. In Amhara, the Regional Disaster Risk Management Bureau reported that, as of late July, nearly 80 percent of the planned 5.6 million hectares had been planted, though in eastern Amhara planting is only around 60 percent. Agricultural activities are also significantly delayed in Tigray. In East and West Hararghe, belg -season moisture stress and continued dryness caused long-cycle meher crops, particularly maize, to wilt or dry up, while some short-cycle meher crops failed to germinate or wilted. Damaged crops are increasingly being used as livestock feed. The poor belg harvests constrained household food stocks and income in several areas of Ethiopia during the lean season. Poor rainfall distribution caused moisture stress during the critical flowering and grain-filling stages, resulting in a below-average belg harvest in several areas. In West Hararghe Zone of Oromia, late-season dry spells and above-average temperatures, compounded by pests, weeds, and crop disease, reduced belg production by an estimated 35 percent below average, with losses exceeding 50 percent in several lowland woredas, according to the Zonal Disaster Risk Management Office. A late rainy season onset followed by a prolonged dry spell also constrained crop development in the belg -producing highlands of Amhara and some areas of Tigray, while moisture stress caused significant yield reductions in areas of Central Ethiopia. Persistently high food prices continue to constrain household purchasing power despite relative month-on-month stability in most markets. According to the Ethiopian Statistics Service (ESS) ,annual headline inflation rose to nearly 14 percent in June, up from 13.4 percent in May. Staple prices were broadly stable between May and June, with localized increases linked to lean season supply constraints and modest declines in some *belg-*producing areas following the harvest. However, prices remained far above normal: maize prices in Sodo in South Ethiopia Region were more than 90 percent above the five-year average, while maize prices in Degahabur in Somali Region were 20 percent above last year and 82 percent above the five-year average. Humanitarian food assistance continued with erratic and low coverage in Amhara in June but was interrupted in Tigray, decreasing support to camp-based IDPs until distributions resumed in July. In Amhara, JEOP and the government of Ethiopia reached more than 177,000 people with food and cash transfers in June. No food distributions were reported in Tigray. Although assistance resumed in July and is expected through August, a potential JEOP pipeline break beginning in September will likely further reduce food assistance delivery.

articles.title: Tchad - Key Message Update : Start of season is delayed in eastern provinces already facing Crisis! (IPC Phase 3!), July 2026 - January 2027
articles.description: Country: Chad Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Crisis! (IPC Phase 3!) outcomes are anticipated through January 2027 in the Assoungha, Kimiti, Wadi Hawar, Dar-Tama, and Kobé departments with expected further deterioration. Refugees, who have lost their livelihoods, continue to arrive in these departments where they account for more than 30 percent of the population. Refugees remain highly dependent on markets and food assistance while increasing pressure on the livelihoods of host populations. Food consumption deficits among host households are worsening further due to the lean season, the persistent delay in the start of the season, and the lack of recovery in key income sources, particularly agricultural labor. The onset of the rainy season is significantly delayed in several provinces, particularly in the Sahelian zone. As of July 10, the season had not yet started in Lac and Kanem provinces or in northern Bahr El-Ghazal, Batha, Ouaddaï, and Wadi Fira. Delays of 10 to 30 days have been observed in Sila and Hadjer Lamis and, farther south, in Salamat, Moyen Chari, and Mandoul. These delays are hindering agricultural activities and agricultural labor, which are key income sources for poor households. The resulting decline in purchasing power is forcing households to accept in-kind payments, often on credit, sell productive assets (including additional livestock among pastoral households), and/or take on debt. Due to insufficient income, household demand for cereals in markets is atypically low, resulting in an atypical decline in prices despite the lean season. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes currently observed in Lac Province are expected to persist through January 2027 due to insufficient food stocks and income , except in the department of Wayi, which is expected to experience Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes between October and January 2027 as harvests improve food consumption. The delayed onset of the season and attacks by armed terrorist groups are contributing to deteriorating livelihoods and declining household income and purchasing power. Food consumption deficits are worsening further among internally displaced persons (IDPs) and host populations. Ongoing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes in northern Kanem and Bahr El-Ghazal provinces are expected to persist through September due to the extension of the pastoral lean season following the delayed onset of the rainy season. Milk production is not expected to recover until after September, while livestock maintenance costs remain high. Market-dependent households are experiencing deterioration in most of their income sources and purchasing power continues to weaken, pushing them to resort to atypical sales of productive assets. The influx of refugees and returnees increased significantly in June, reaching 6,337 arrivals (compared with an average of 2,120 per month between March and May), following clashes on June 28 and 29, 2026, around Kulbus, Sudan. According to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), more than 3,000 arrivals were recorded in Koulbous, on the Chadian side of the border, between June 30 and July 13, 2026. This brought the cumulative number of new Sudanese refugees arriving in the eastern provinces since April 2023 to 936,900, of whom 642,850 have been relocated farther into these provinces. These arrivals are increasing market demand and putting additional pressure on local livelihoods and host-community resources. The security situation remains a key driver of food insecurity in several provinces of Chad. According to ACLED, Chad recorded 23 security incidents between June 17 and July 17, 2026, resulting in 23 deaths. Most incidents (48 percent) occurred in the eastern provinces, particularly Wadi Fira and Ouaddaï. These incidents involved the army's efforts to disarm armed refugees, as well as clashes between agropastoralists around water points. Lac Province accounted for 22 percent of security incidents, including the looting of food supplies (particularly flour, rice, and oil) following Boko Haram attacks, such as the July 7 attack on the village of Foulatari in Fouli. These incidents are creating a climate of fear, driving population displacement and disrupting livelihoods.

articles.title: Afghanistan | Northern - Earthquake - DREF Operational Update #4 (MDRAF019), 7 August 2026
articles.description: Country: Afghanistan Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date of event 03-11-2025 What happened, where and when? On 3 November 2025, a magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck northern Afghanistan near the Balkh-Samangan border at a depth of 28 km. The tremor was felt widely across northern and central Afghanistan and as far as Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The earthquake caused 26 deaths and 1,172 injuries in communities that were already highly vulnerable. Verified assessments recorded 3,027 families with damaged homes across the affected districts, of which 874 homes were destroyed and 2,153 damaged. Broader United Nations assessments estimate that nearly 4,000 families were affected overall, alongside 91 schools and 18 water sources rendered unusable (OCHA, Humanitarian Update, January 2026). The earthquake also disrupted essential services, including health facilities, and temporarily blocked the Balkh-Kabul highway, exposing the fragility of access routes and the risk of secondary hazards such as landslides and rockfall. The earthquake triggered a mountain collapse in the Tangi Ashburnham Valley, which temporarily obstructed the Balkh-Kabul highway with falling rocks. Clearance operations have since been completed, and the route has reopened to traffic. Prior to the earthquake, the affected provinces already hosted significant numbers of vulnerable people, including an estimated 9,129 internally displaced persons (IDPs), 12,032 IDP returnees, and more than 16,404 people returning from abroad. In total, approximately 220,311 people; 52 per cent male and 48 per cent female were living in highly vulnerable conditions. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) estimates that around 1.53 million people experienced strong ground shaking in areas surrounding the epicenter. The event caused widespread fear among affected communities and damaged residential buildings and community infrastructure across multiple districts. In response, Provincial Disaster Management Committees (PDMCs) in Balkh and Samangan convened emergency coordination meetings on 3 November and mobilized joint inter-agency assessment teams to determine the scale of the impact and identify urgent humanitarian needs. Winter conditions have since compounded the crisis: between 21 and 23 January 2026, heavy snowfall, storms, and avalanches affected 15 provinces—including Balkh and Samangan—further isolating communities and constraining access to essential supplies and services (OCHA, Humanitarian Update, January 2026). In response to the earthquake, the IFRC immediately released CHF 100,000 Emergency Advance Payment under DREF procedures to enable ARCS's initial response. The subsequent DREF grant allocation brought the total DREF allocation to CHF 1,000,000. The earthquake response falls within the scope of the Afghanistan Earthquake Emergency Appeal (MDRAF019), launched on 3 September 2025 at CHF 25 million and revised upward to CHF 30 million following the northern earthquake, which supports ARCS's wider relief and early recovery efforts. This Operational Update reports on the first six months of the DREF grant implementation; further details on the DREF and Emergency Appeal is provided under the IFRC Network Actions section below.

articles.title: Djibouti Storm Surge 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRDJ010)
articles.description: Country: Djibouti Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date of event 27-07-2026 What happened, where and when? In the locality of Mouloud, Dhikil region was struck by a severe windstorm accompanied by heavy rainfall on 27 July 2026, between 5:00 and 6:00 p.m. This was the second storm to affect the locality within a few days, following an earlier event on 24 July 2026, which caused no major damage. Preliminary reports indicate that more than 4160 people (693HH) were affected with approximately 290 households (1740 people) that have seen their houses partially of fully demolished. The disaster has resulted in two fatalities (an elderly man and an infant) and 10 injuries, including three children and 168 HH fully displaced. The injured were evacuated to the Ali Sabieh Regional Hospital and Dikhil Hospital for medical treatment. Concurrently, extra ordinary temperature rise has been observed with temperatures going for beyond 42 degrees in recent days, with the weekly forecast ranging between 42 to 45 degrees of centigrade. https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/forecast/sfn9tysge#?date=2026-07-30 . This situation is exacerbated by heavy storms posing more risk to the displaced and other weak shelters. Several isolated domestic fires are also reported in the rise due the heavy winds, and the extra ordinary temperature rises. The communities living in Djibouti-Ville, especially Balbala and Boulaos communes, which are densely populated areas, characterized by informal settlements, with limited resources to cope with extreme heat, poor housing, reduced access to cooling, these population are highly impacted by intense heat stress and extreme mugginess during long hot spells from May through September, exposing them to negative coping strategies and more secondary impacts. The storm affected communities in areas like Dikhil are the most exposed to storms likely to continue concurrently with the high temperatures. The effect of the heatwave on life and wellbeing is higher now where families have been displaced or have severe damages to their houses when these are first layer of protection in heatwaves context. As much as this IFRC-DREF is for now essentially triggered by the effects of the storm, the response strategy will have a multi hazard approach to both the rising heat wave, storms in Dhikil. Noting that heatwaves impact is already witnessed and projected to get worse especially in Djibouti densely populated suburbs of Balbala and Boulaos , extending to regions already facing storms specifically Mouloud, in Dikhil, the key messages for early warning and early actions will be disseminated to inform the preventive measures.

articles.title: Lesotho | Drought induced food insecurity - Final Report (MDRLS008)
articles.description: Country: Lesotho Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. SITUATION ANALYSIS Description of the crisis Overview of the 2022/2023–2024/2025 Rainy Season Conditions and Impacts The 2021/2022 and 2022/2023 rainy seasons in Lesotho were marked by excessive rainfall that disrupted farming, damaged crops, and reduced agricultural productivity, resulting in poor harvests, lower food production, and increased food insecurity nationwide. Beyond damaging crops, the heavy rains also destroyed stored food supplies and damaged critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, and irrigation systems, particularly in the rural districts of Maseru and Quthing. These impacts disrupted livelihoods, limited access to essential services, and further deepened food insecurity among vulnerable communities. While communities were still recovering from the previous years (2021 to 2023) heavy rainfall events, the country was hit by El Niño-induced drought in 2023/2024 and this period was characterized by late onset of rains and recurrent heatwaves from October 2023 to early 2024/2025, further worsening the already fragile livelihoods and living conditions. For the past three years, the country has continued to experience persistent and compounding climatic shocks, including periods of excessive rainfall (2022–2024) followed by severe drought (2024/2025) conditions, which disrupted agriculture, weakened livelihoods, and worsened rural livelihoods, increasing food insecurity and slowing recovery efforts. In July 2024, over 22% of the Lesotho population (approximately 335,000 people) were estimated to be food insecure (LVAC Report 2024) and required urgent humanitarian assistance. Alongside drought related food insecurity, increase in staple food prices and declining livestock production have reduced household purchasing power and weakened livelihoods, further increasing vulnerability and worsening food insecurity. Livestock farmers in the southern side of the country were also affected by livestock disease outbreak “ Blue Tongue,” which resulted in losses of around 200 sheep and goats. The situation further undermined household incomes that depend on wool and mohair production. As a result, many vulnerable households resorted to negative coping strategies, including selling productive assets to either meet their basic needs or restore their damaged houses. The worsening conditions in Lesotho led to a crisis that prompted the government to declare a state of emergency in July 2024, to address widespread food insecurity, livelihood disruptions, and to mobilize urgent humanitarian response.
